Accompanying; conjoined; attending. It has pleased our wise Creator to annex to several objects, as also to several of our thoughts, a concomitant pleasure. Locke.
In company with others; unitedly; concurrently. Bp. pears on.
Agreement of words with one another, in gender, number, person,or case.
A kind of buggy having a body with low sides, and side springs.
Capable of according; agreeing; harmonious.
Concord; agreement. [Obs.] as ch lam.
Agreement. W. mon ta gu.
Agreeing; correspondent; harmonious; consonant. Were every one employed in points concordant to their natures,professions, and arts, commonwealths would rise up of themselves. SirT. brow ne
In a concordant manner.
The compiler of a concordance.
To unite in one mass or body; to incorporate. [Archaic.] Jer. Taylor.
Union of things in one mass or body. [R.] Dr. H. More.
To create at the same time. If God did concreate grace with Adam. Jer. Taylor.
The act of burning different things together. [Obs.]
A growing together; the collection or mass formed by concretion, or natural union. [Obs.]The concrement of a pebble or flint. Sir M. Hale
Coalescence of particles; growth; increase by the addition of particles. [R.] Sir W. ra leigh.
Capable of being changed from a liquid to a solid state. [Obs.]They formed a . . . fixed concrescible oil. four croy (Trans. ).
Growing together, or into union; uniting. [R.] Eclec. Rev.
A term designating both a quality and the subject in which it exists; a concrete term. The concretes "father" and "son" have, or might have, the abstracts"paternity" and "filiety". J. S. Mill.
In a concrete manner.
The quality of being concrete.
A rounded mass or nodule produced by an aggregation of the material around a center; as, the calcareous concretions common in beds of clay.
Concretionary.
Pertaining to, or formed by, concretion or aggregation;producing or containing concretions.
Promoting concretion. Sir T. brow ne.
In a concrete manner.
A mass formed by concretion. [Obs.] Johnson.
To grow together. [Obs.] sp en ser.
A joint accusation.
The practice of concubinage. [Obs.] Strype.
A plea, in which it is alleged that the woman suing for dower was not lawfully married to the man in whose lands she seeks to been do wed, but that she was his concubine.
Of or pertaining to concubinage.
Concubinary. The married and concubinarian, as well as looser clergy. mil man.
Relating to concubinage; living in concubinage.
Concubinage. [Obs.] Johnson.
To tread or trample under foot. [Obs.] Bp. mon ta gu --Con`cul*ca"tion (, n. [Obs.]
Sexual lust; morbid carnal passion. Concupiscence like a pestilence walk eth in darkness. hor ne.
Having sexual lust; libidinous; lustful; lecherous; salacious. Johnson.
Relating to concupiscence. [Obs.] Johnson.
Concupiscent. [Obs.]
The state of being concupiscible. [Obs.]
Concupiscence.
Concurrence.
Meeting in one point.
With concurrence; unitedly.
The state or quality of being concurrent; concurrence.
Agreeing. Concurring figure (Geom.), one which, being laid on another, exactly meets every part of it, or one which correspond ends with another in all its parts.
To force (a person) to do something, or give up something, by intimidation; to coerce. whart on.
A violent shock or agitation. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.
A condition of lowered functional activity, without visible structural change, produced in an organ by a shock, as by fall or blow; as, a concussion of the brain.
Having the power or quality of shaking or agitating. Johnson.
To con, as a ship.
To doom to be taken for public use, under the right of eminent domain.
Worthy of condemnation; blamable; culpable.
Condemning; containing or imposing condemnation or censure; as,a condemnatory sentence or decree.
One who condemns or censures.
Capability of being condensed.
Capable of being condensed; as, vapor is condensable.
Made dense; condensed. Water . . . thickened or condensate. peach am.
The act or process of reducing, by depression of temperature or increase of pressure, etc., to another and denser form, as gas to the condition of a liquid or steam to water.
Having the property of condensing.

To reduce into another and denser form, as by cold or pressure;as, to condense gas into a liquid form, or steam into water. Condensed milk, milk reduced to the consistence of very thick cream by evaporation (usually with addition of sugar) for preservation and transportation.-- Condensing engine, a steam engine in which the steam is condensed after having exerted its force on the piston.
An apparatus for receiving and condensing the volatile products of distillation to a liquid or solid form, by cooling.
Capable of being condensed; as, a gas condensible to a liquid by cold.
One who watches shoals of fish; a balker. See Balker.
Condescension. [Obs.]
In a condescending manner. atter bury.

The act of condescending; voluntary descent from one's rank or dignity in intercourse with an inferior; courtesy toward inferiors. It forbids pride . . . and commands humility, modesty, and condescension to others. tillot son. Such a dignity and condescension . . . as are suitable to a superior nature. Addison.
An act of condescension. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.

Merit, ac gu ired by works, which can claim reward on the score of general benevolence. Such a worthiness of condignity, and proper merit of the heavenly glory, cannot be found in any the best, most perfect, and excellent of created beings. Bp. Bull.
According to merit.
Agreeableness to deserts; suitableness.

Something used to give relish to food, and to gratify the taste; a pung me nt and appetizing substance, as pepper or mustard;seasoning. As for radish and the like, they are for condiments, and not for nourishment. Bacon.
A schoolfellow; a fellow-student. [R.]
Preserved; pickled. [Obs.] Burton.

A clause in a contract, or agreement, which has for its object to suspend, to defeat, or in some way to modify, the principal obligation; or, in case of a will, to suspend, revoke, or modify ade vise or bequest. It is also the case of a future uncertain event,which may or may not happen, and on the occurrence or non-occurrence of which, the accomplishment, recission, or modification of an obligation or testamentary disposition is made to depend. Blount. tom lins. Bouvier. whart on. Equation of condition. (Math.) See under equation.-- On or Upon condition (that), used for if in introducing condition al sentences. "Upon condition thou wilt swear to pay him tribute . . . thou shalt be placed as viceroy under him." sh ak.-- Conditions of sale, the terms on which it is proposed to sell property by auction; also, the instrument containing or expressing these terms.

Expressing a condition or supposition; as, a conditional word,mode, or tense. A conditional proposition is one which asserts the dependence of one categorical proposition on another. wh ately. The words hypothetical and conditional may be . . . used synonymously. J. S. Mill.
The quality of being conditional, or limited; limitation by certain terms.
In a conditional manner; subject to a condition or conditions;not absolutely or positively. sh ak.
Conditional. [Obs.]Barak's answer is faithful, though conditionate. Bp. Hall.
Conditionally. [Obs.]
A repository for holding things; a hi nd ing place.
To concur; to agree. [Burlesque]
Expressing condolence. Smart.
To express sympathetic sorrow; to grieve in sympathy; --followed by with. Your friends would have cause to rejoice, rather than condole with you. Sir W. Temple.
Expression of sympathy with another in sorrow or grief. Their congratulations and their condolences. Steele. A special mission of condolence. ma caul ay.
One who condoles.

Forgiveness, either express or implied, by a husband of his wife or by a wife of her husband, for a breach of marital duty, as adultery, with an implied condition that the offense shall not be repeated. Bouvier. whart on.
To pardon; to overlook the offense of; esp., to forgive for a violation of the marriage law; -- said of either the husband or the wife.
A very large bird of the Vulture family (sarcorhamphus gryph us), found in the most elevated parts of the Andes.
A military adventurer of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, who sold his services, and those of his followers, to any party in any contest.

To lead or tend, esp. with reference to a favorable or desirable result; to contribute; -- usually followed by to or toward. He was sensible how much such a union would conduce to the happiness of both. ma caul ay. The reasons you allege do more conduce To the hot passion ofdistemper'd blood. sh ak.
Conducive; tending. Conducent to the good success of this business. Abp. Laud.
The state or quality of being conducible; conducibleness. Bp. wilk ins.
Conducive; tending; contributing. Bacon. All his laws are in themselves conducible to the temporal interest of them that observe them. be nt ley.
Quality of being conducible.
In a manner to promote. [R.]
Loading or tending; helpful; contributive; tending to promote. However conducive to the good or our country. Addison.
The quality of conducing.
To serve as a medium for conveying; to transmit, as heat,light, electricity, etc.
Conducting power; -- the reciprocal of resistance. A suggested unit is the mho, the reciprocal of the ohm.
Capable of being conducted.

Transmission through, or by means of, a conductor; also,conductivity.[The] communication [of heat] from one body to another when they are in contact, or through a homogenous body from particle to particle,constitutes conduction. am er. Cyc.
Having the quality or power of conducting; as, the conductive tissue of a pistil. The ovarian walls . . . are seen to be distinctly conductive. Goodale(Gray's Bot. ).

The quality or power of conducting, or of receiving and transmitting, as, the conductivity of a nerve. Thermal conductivity(Physics), the quantity of heat that passes in unit time through unit area of plate whose thickness is unity, when its opposite faces differ in temperature by one degree. J. D. Everett.-- thermo metic conductivity (Physics), the thermal conductivity when the unit of heat employed is the heat required to raise unit volume of the substance one degree.
The leader or director of an orchestra or chorus.
Having the property of conducting. [R.]
A woman who leads or directs; a directress.

A system of electric traction, esp. for light railways, in which the actuating current passes along a wire or rail laid in an underground conduit, from which the current is "picked up" by a plow or other device fixed to the car or electric locomotive. hence conduit railway.
Folded lengthwise along the midrib, the upper face being within; -- said of leaves or petals in vernation or æst iv at ion.
A doubling together or folding; a duplication. [R.]
See Cundurango.
A variety of the mineral domeykite, or copper arsenide, from the con durra mine in Cornwall, England.

Of or pertaining to a condyle. Condylar foramen (Anat.), af or men in front of each condyle of the occipital bone; -- sometimes called the anterior condylar foramen when a second, or posterior,foramen is present behind the condyle, as often happens in man.
A bony prominence; particularly, an eminence at the end of ab one bearing a rounded articular surface; -- sometimes applied also to a concave articular surface.
Shaped like or pertaining to a condyle.
An arthropod.

A solid of the form described by the revolution of a right-angled triangle about one of the sides adjacent to the right angle; -- called also a right cone. More generally, any solid having a vertical point and bounded by a surface which is described by a straight line always passing through that vertical point; a solid having a circle for its base and tapering to a point or vertex.
A friction clutch with conical bearing surfaces.
A pulley for driving machines, etc., having two or more parts or steps of different diameters; a pulley having a conical shape.
Consisting of a series of parallel cones, each made up of many concentric cones closely packed together; -- said of a kind of structure sometimes observed in sedimentary rocks.

A large hemipterous insect of the family Reduviidæ, often found in houses, esp. in the southern and western United States. It bit es severely, and is one of the species called kissing bugs. It is also called big bedbug.

Any plant of the genus Rudbeckia; -- so called from the cone-shaped disk of the flower head. Also, any plant of the related gene rara ti bi da and Brauneria, the latter usually known as purple coneflower.
See Conine.
A rabbit. See Cony.
Familiar talk or conversation. [Colloq.]
To talk familiarly together; to chat; to prattle. I shall not ask Jean ja ques Rousseau If birds confabulate or no. Cowper.
Familiar talk; easy, unrestrained, unceremonious conversation. Friends' confabulations are comfortable at all times, as fire in winter. Burton.
Of the nature of familiar talk; in the form of a dialogue. Weever.
One of a fraternity of seculars, also called Penitents.
A form of marriage among the Romans, in which an offering of bread was made, in presence of the high priest and at least ten witnesses.
Fated or decreed with something else. [R.] A. Tucker.
A comfit; a confection. [Obs.]At supper eat a pippin roasted and sweetened with sugar of roses and car away confects. Harvey.
A soft solid made by incorporating a medicinal substance or substances with sugar, sirup, or honey.
A confectioner. [Obs.]He will take your daughters to be confectionaries, and to be cooks. 1Sam. viii. 13.
A highly refined sugar in impalpable powder, esp. suited to confectioners' uses.
Pertaining to the art of making sweetmeats. [Obs.] Beaumont.
Same as Confiture. [Obs.]
To confederate. [Obs.] Sir T. North.
A combination of two or more persons to commit an unlawful act,or to do a lawful act by unlawful means. See Conspiracy.

Of or pertaining to the government of the eleven southern states of the United States which (1860-1865) attempted to establish an independent nation styled the Confederate States of America; as,the Confederate congress; Confederate money.
A confederate.
Of or pertaining to a confederation.
A confederate. graft on.
To have discourse; to consult; to compare views; to deliberate. fest us, when he had conferred with the council, answered. Acts xxv.12. You shall hear us confer of this. sh ak.
A stated meeting of preachers and others, invested with authority to take cognizance of ecclesiastical matters.
Relating to conference. [R.] Clarke.
Capable of being conferred.
Same as Conferee.
Closely united by the coalescence, or sticking together, of contiguous faces, as in the case of the cotyledons of the live-oak acorn.
Any unbranched, slender, green plant of the fresh-water algae. The word is frequently used in a wider sense.
Belonging to the confervae.
Like, or related to, the confervae. loud on.
Pertaining to confervae; consisting of, or resembling, the confervae. Yon exiguous pool's confervous scum. O. W. Holmes.
One who confesses to a priest. [Obs.] Bacon.
One who makes a confession. [Obs.] Bp. Hall.
By confession; without denial. [Written also confess ly.]
One who makes a confession.

The act of disclosing sins or faults to a priest in order to obtain sacramental absolution. Auricular confession . . . or the private and special confession of sins to a priest for the purpose of obtaining his absolution. hall am.

The recess, seat, or inclosed place, where a priest sits to hear confessions; often a small structure furnished with a seat for the priest and with a window or aperture so that the penitent who is outside may whisper into the priest's ear without being seen by him or heard by others.
An exaggerated estimate of the importance of giving full as sent to any particular formula of the Christian faith. sha ff.
A priest hearing, or sitting to hear, confession. [R.] Boucher
A confessional. [Obs.] Johnson.
One professing a certain faith. Bp. mon ta gu.
The act or state of suffering persecution for religious faith. Our duty to contend even to confessorship. J. H. new man.
See co fessed ly.
Bonbons; sweetmeats; confections; also, plaster or paper imitations of, or substitutes for, bonbons, often used by carnival revelers, at weddings, etc.

To put faith (in); to repose confidence; to trust; -- usually followed by in; as, the prince confides in his ministers. By thy command I rise or fall, In thy protection I confide. Byron. Judge before friendships, then confide till death. Young.
See Confidant. South. dry den.
In confidence; in reliance on secrecy.
With confidence; with strong assurance; positively.
The quality of being confident.
One who confides.
That confides; trustful; unsuspicious.-- Con*fid"ing*ly, adv.-- Con*fid"ing*ness, n.

To take form or position, as the parts of a complex structure;to agree with a pattern. Known by the name of uniformity; Where pyramids to pyramids re late and the whole fabric doth configurate. Jordan.

Relative position or aspect of the planets; the face of the horoscope, according to the relative positions of the planets at anytime. They [astrologers] undertook . . . to determine the course of a man'scharacter and life from the configuration of the stars at the moment of his birth. Whewell.
To arrange or dispose in a certain form, figure, or shape. be nt ley.
Capable of being confined, restricted, or limited. Not confinable to any limits. Bp. Hall.

To restrain within limits; to restrict; to limit; to bound; to shut up; to inclose; to keep close. Now let not nature's hand Keep the wild flood confined! let order die! sh ak. He is to confine himself to the compass of numbers and the slavery of rhyme. dry den. To be confined, to be in childbed.
Without limitation or end; boundless. sh ak.
One who, or that which, limits or restrains.
Community of limits; contiguity. [R.] Bailey.
To administer the rite of confirmation to. See Confirmation, 3. Those which are thus confirmed are thereby supposed to be fit for admission to the sacrament. ham mo nd.
That may be confirmed.
Confirmation. [Obs.]

A rite supplemental to baptism, by which a person is admitted,through the laying on of the hands of a bishop, to the full privileges of the church, as in the Roman Catholic, the episcopal church, etc. This ordinance is called confirmation, because they who duly receive it are confirmed or strengthened for the fulfillment of their christian duties, by the grace therein bestowed upon them. Hook.
Tending confirm or establish. sher wood.-- Con*firm"a*tive*ly, adv.
One who, or that which, confirms; a confirmer. Sir T. brow ne.
Serving to confirm; corroborative. A fact confirmatory of the conclusion. I. Taylor.
With confirmation.
A fixed state.
One to whom an ut hing is confirmed.
One who, or that which, confirms, establishes, or ratifies; one who corroborates. sh ak.
In a confirming manner.
Capable of being confiscated; liable to forfeiture.
Seized and appropriated by the government to the public use;forfeited. Lest that your goods too soon be confiscate. sh ak.
The act or process of taking property or condemning it to betaken, as forfeited to the public use. The confiscations following a subdued rebellion. hall am.
One who confiscates. Burke.
Effecting confiscation; characterized by confiscations."Confiscatory and exterminatory periods." Burke.
Same as Comfit. [Obs.]
One who confesses his sins and faults. [Obs.]
A form of prayer in which public confession of sins is made.

The state or quality of being congenial; natural affinity;adaptation; suitableness. Sir J. reyn olds. If congeniality of tastes could have made a marriage happy, that union should have been thrice blessed. Motley.
To fix; to fasten. [Obs.] sh ak.
Act of fastening. [Obs.]
Burning together in a common flame. [R.] "The conflagrant mass." Milton.
A fire extending to many objects, or over a large space; a general burning.
To blow together; to bring together; to collect; to fuse together; to join or weld; to consolidate.
A blowing together, as of many instruments in a concert, or of many fires in a foundry. [R.] Bacon.
Being in conflict or collision, or in opposition; contending;contradictory; incompatible; contrary; opposing.
Tending to conflict; conflicting. Sir W. Hamilton.
The tendency of fluids to run together. [R.] boy le.
Inclined to flow or run together. --Con*flux"i*ble*ness, n.
Having the same foci; as, confocal quadrics.
Of the same form; similar in import; conformable. Bacon.
The quality of being conformable; conformability.
With conformity or in conformity; suitably; agreeably.
Conformity. [R.] mar st on.
Having the same form. [R.]
An apparatus for taking the conformation of anything, as of the head for fitting a hat, or, in craniometry, finding the largest horizontal area of the head.
One who conforms; one who complies with established forms or doctrines.
One who conforms or complies; esp., one who conforms to the church of England, or to the Established Church, as distinguished from a dissenter or nonconformist.
The act of strengthening. [Obs.] Bacon.
Extremely; odiously; detestably. [Colloq.] "Confoundedly sick."Goldsmith.
The state of being confounded.
One who confounds.
Broken in pieces; severed. [Obs.]
Broken; uneven. [Obs.] "Confragose cataracts." Evelyn.
A society or body of men united for some purpose, or in some profession; a brotherhood.
Fellow member of a fraternity; intimate associate.
A rubbing together; friction. [Obs.] Bacon.
A confrère. [Obs.] Weever.
Act of confronting. H. sw in bur ne.
Same as Affronté.
One who confronts.
dealing with (a person or problem) directly; taking the bull by the horns. Syn. -- braving, coping with, grappling, tackling.[WordNet 1.5 +PJC]
The act of confronting; the state of being face to face.
Of, or relating to, Confucius, the great Chinese philosopher and teacher. -- n.

The political morality taught by Confucius and his disciples,which forms the basis of the Chinese jurisprudence and education. it can hardly be called a religion, as it does not inculcate the worship of any god. S. W. Williams.
A follower of Confucius; a Confucian. S. W. Williams.
Confused, disturbed. [Obs.] Chaucer.
Capability of being confused.
Capable of being confused.
Mixed; confounded. [Obs.] Baret.
In a confused manner.
A state of confusion. nor ris.
Confusedly; obscurely. [Obs.]
Confusing; having a tendency to confusion. Bp. Hall.
That may be confuted.
One who undertakes to confute. Milton.
The act or process of confuting; refutation. "For the edification of some and the confutation of others." Bp. hor ne.
Adapted or designed to confute. Bp. war burton
To overwhelm by argument; to refute conclusively; to prove or show to be false or defective; to overcome; to silence.
Confutation. [Obs.] Milton.
One who confutes or disproves.
An abbreviation of Congius.
To take leave with the customary civilities; to bow or courtesy.
Permissible; done lawfully; as, entry congeable.
To grow hard, stiff, or thick, from cold or other causes; to become solid; to freeze; to cease to flow; to run cold; to be chilled.
Capable of being congealed. --Con*geal"a*ble*ness, n.
The state of being congealed. Dr. H. More.
See Congé, Conge. [Obs.]
A thing of the same genus, species, or kind; a thing allied in nature, character, or action.
Similarity of origin; affinity. [Obs.] Dr. H. More.
Allied in origin or cause; congeneric; as, congenerous diseases. [Obs.] Sir T. brow ne.
The state or quality of being congenial; natural affinity;adaptation; suitableness. Sir J. reyn olds.
To make congenial. [R.]
In a congenial manner; as, congenially married or employed.
Congeniality.
Congeneric. [Obs.]
Existing at, or dating from, birth; pertaining to one from birth; born with one; connate; const it ut in al; natural; as, ac on genital deformity. See Connate.
In a congenital manner.
Congenital; connate; inborn. See Congenital. [Obs.]Many conclusions, of moral and intellectual truths, seem . . . to be congenite with us. Sir M. Hale.
The conger eel; -- called also congeree. Conger sea (Zoöl.),the sea eel; a large species of eel (Conger vulgar is), which sometimes grows to the length of ten feet.
A collection of particles or bodies into one mass; a heap; an aggregation.
To cause an overfullness of the blood vessels (esp. the capillaries) of an organ or part.
Crowded together. Gray.

Overfullness of the capillary and other blood vessels, etc., in any locality or organ (often producing other morbid symptoms); local hyper as, arterial congestion; venous congestion; congestion of the lungs.
Pertaining to, indicating, or attended with, congestion in somepart of the body; as, a congestive fever.
A present, as of corn, wine, or oil, made by a Roman emperor to the soldiers or the people; -- so called because measured to each ina congius. Addison.
A liquid measure containing about three quarts.
To turn to ice; to freeze. [Obs.] Sir T. brow ne.
The act or process of changing into ice, or the state of being converted to ice; a freezing; congelation; also, a frost. Bacon.
Collected into, or forming, a rounded mass or ball; as, the conglobate [lymphatic] glands; conglobate flowers.
To gather into a ball; to collect into a round mass. Then founded, then conglobed Like things to like. Milton.
To gather into a small round mass.
Closely crowded together; den sly clustered; as, conglomerate flowers. Gray.
The act or process of gathering into a mass; the state of being thus collected; collection; accumulation; that which is conglomerated; a mixed mass. Bacon.
A variety of vegetable casein, resembling legumin, and found in almonds, rye, wheat, etc.
Cementing together; uniting closely; causing to adhere;promoting healing, as of a wound or a broken bone, by adhesion of the parts.
Glued together; united, as by some adhesive substance.
A gluing together; a joining by means of some tenacious substance; junction; union. Conglutination of parts separated by a wound. ar bu th not.
Conglutinant.
A group of artificial dyes with an affinity for vegetable fibers, so that no mordant is required. Most of them are azo compounds derived from benzidine or tolidine. Called also benzidin ed yes.

An artificial red dye from which the Congo group received its name. It is also widely used either in aqueous solution or as test paper (Congo paper) for the detection of free acid, which turns it blue.
An amphibian (Amphiuma means) of the order Urodela, found in the southern United States. See Amphiuma.
Rejoicing together; congratulatory. With like joy Congratulant approached him. Milton.

To address with expressions of sympathetic pleasure on account of some happy event affecting the person addressed; to wish joy to. It is the king's most sweet pleasure and affection to congratulate the princess at her pavilion. sh ak. To congratulate one's self, to rejoice; to feel satisfaction; to consider one's self happy or fortunate.
The act of congratulating; an expression of sympathetic pleasure. With infinite congratulations for our safe arrival. Dr. J. Scott.
One who offers congratulation. Milton.
Expressive of sympathetic joy; as, a congratulatory letter.
To agree. [bs.] sh ak.
To salute mutually. [Obs.]
Collected; compact; close. [R.] Bacon.
The whole body of the Jewish people; -- called also congregation of the Lord. It is a sin offering for the congregation. Lev. iv. 21.
One who belongs to a Congregational church or society; one who holds to Congregationalism.
A coming or bringing together, as in a public meeting, in a dispute, in the act of comparing, or in sexual intercourse. [R.] Jer. Taylor.

Of or pertaining to a congress, especially, to the Congress of the United States; as, congressional debates. Congressional and official labor. E. Everett. Congressional District, one of the divisions into which a State is periodically divided (according to population), each of which is entitled to elect a Representative to the Congress of the united states.
Encountering, or coming together. Sir T. brow ne.
A member of the Congress of the United States, esp. of the house of Representatives.
See under Rocket.
To agree; to be suitable. [Obs.] sh ak.
Suitableness of one thing to another; agreement; consistency. Holland.
Congruence. Congruency of lines. (Geom.) See Complex of lines,under Complex, n.
Possessing congruity; suitable; agreeing; corresponding. The congruent and harmonious fitting of parts in a sentence. B. jon son. Congruent figures (Geom.), concurring figures.
See Congruity.
Coincidence, as that of lines or figures laid over one another.

Suitable or concordant; accordant; fit; harmonious;correspondent; consistent. Not congruous to the nature of epic poetry. Blair. It is no ways congruous that God should be always frightening men into an acknowledgment of the truth. atter bury.
In a congruous manner.
A vegetable alkaloid found with conine in the poison hemlock(Conium macula tum). It is a white crystalline substance, C8H17NO,easily convertible into conine.
Same as Conine.
A conic section.
Conicalness.
In the form of a cone.
State or quality of being conical.
A combining form, meaning somewhat resembling a cone; as,conico-cylindrical, resembling a cone and a cylinder; coni co-hemispherical; coni co-subulate.
Same as Conoidal.
A peculiar kind of reproductive cell found in certain fungi,and often containing zoöspores.
A tree or shrub bearing cones; one of the order Coniferae,which includes the pine, cypress, and (according to some) the yew.
A glucoside extracted from the cambium layer of coniferous trees as a white crystalline substance.
Cone-shaped; conical.
See Conine.
Same as Olibene.

A powerful and very poisonous vegetable alkaloid found in the hemlock (Conium macula tum) and extracted as a colorless oil, C8H17N,of strong repulsive odor and acrid taste. It is regarded as a derivative of piperidine and likewise of one of the collidin es. it occasions a gradual paralysis of the motor nerves. Called also coniine, coneine, conia, etc. See Conium, 2.
One of the Conirostres.
Belonging to the Conirostres.
A tribe of perching birds, including those which have a strong conical bill, as the finches.
See Cognizor.

Originally, a part of the palestra, or gymnasium among the greeks; either the place where sand was stored for use in sprinkling the wrestlers, or the wrestling ground itself. Hence, a part of the orchestra of the Greek theater.
A magnesian variety of dolomite.
A genus of biennial, poisonous, white-flowered, umbelliferous plants, bearing ribbed fruit ("seeds") and decompound leaves.
To throw together, or to throw. [Obs.] Bp. mon ta gu.
One who guesses or conjectures. [Obs.]A great conjector at other men by their writings. Milton.

In a conjoint manner; un tit ed ly; jointly; together. Sir T. brow ne.

Shouting together for joy; rejoicing together. [R.] nea le.
Belonging to marriage; suitable or appropriate to the marriage state or to married persons; matrimonial; connubial. "conjugal affection." Milton.
The conjugal state; sexual intercourse. [R.] Milton.
In a conjugal manner; matrimonially; connubially.
In single pairs; coupled.

To join, unite, or cohere; to have a close relation; as, one line of railroad connects with another; one argument connect with another.

Connecting, or adapted to connect; involving connection. Connection tissue (Anat.) See Conjunctive tissue, under Conjunctive.
In conn junction; jointly.
One who, or that which, connects; as:(a) A flexible tube for connecting the ends of glass tubes in pneumatic experiments.(b) A device for holding two parts of an electrical conductor in contact.
A marine European fish (cr en il abrus me lops); also, the related american cunner. See Cunner.
To connect. Sir M. Hale.
Connection. See Connection.

The shotproof pilot house of a war vessel.
Corrupt or guilty assent to wrongdoing, not involving actual participation in, but knowledge of, and failure to prevent or oppose it.

To connote; to suggest or designate (something) as additional;to include; to imply. ham mo nd.

Implying an attribute. See Connote. Connotative term, one which de notes a subject and implies an attribute. J. S. Mill.
In a connotative manner; expressing connotation.

To imply as an attribute. The word "white" denotes all white things, as snow, paper, the foam of the sea, etc., and ipm lies, or as it was termed by the schoolmen,connotes, the attribute "whiteness." J. S. Mill.
Of or pertaining to marriage, or the marriage state; conjugal;nuptial. Nor Eve the rites Mysterious of connubial love refused. Milton. Kind, connubial tenderness. Goldsmith.
The quality of being connubial; something characteristics of the conjugal state; an expression of connubial tenderness. Some connu biali ties which had begun to pass between Mr. and Mrs. B. Dickens.
A reckoning together. [R.] por son.

See Cognizant. [Obs.]
See Cognizor. [Obs.]
Nutritious by force of habit; -- said of certain kinds of food.[Obs.] cr abb.

Capable of being conquered or subdued. South.-- Con"quer*a*ble*ness, n.
A woman who conquers. fair fax.
One who conquers. The Conqueror (Eng. Hist.). William then or man (1027-1067) who invaded England, defeated Harold in the battle of Hastings, and was crowned king, in 1066.
The acquiring of property by other means than by inheritance;acquisition. black stone.
A game for two, played with 40 cards, in which each player tries to form three or four of a kind or sequences.
Of the same blood; related by birth. Sir T. brow ne.

The relation of person by blood, is distinction from affinity or relation by marriage; blood relationship; as, line al consanguinity; collateral consanguinity. Invoking aid by the ties of consanguinity. pre scott.
A patching together; patchwork. [Obs.] Bailey.
Having a conscience. [R.] "Soft-conscienced men." sh ak.
Without conscience; indifferent to conscience; unscrupulous. Conscienceless and wicked patrons. hook re.
Conscious. [R.] Bacon.
In a conscientious manner; as a matter of conscience; hence;faithfully; accurately; completely.
The quality of being conscientious; a scrupulous regard to the dictates of conscience.
Governed by, or according to, conscience; reasonable; just. Let my debtors have conscionable satisfaction. Sir H. wot ton.
The quality of being conscionable; reasonableness. Johnson.
Reasonably; justly.
In a conscious manner; with knowledge of one's own mental operations or actions.
To enroll; to enlist. [Obs.] E. Hall.

Enrolled; written; registered. Conscript fathers (Rom. Antiq.),the senators of ancient Rome. When certain new senators were first enrolled with the "fathers" the body was called pat res et Conscripti;afterward all were called pat res con scrip ti.
Belonging to, or of the nature of, a conspiration.
Consecrated; devoted; dedicated; sacred. They were assembled in that consecrate place. Bacon.
Consecrator.

The act or ceremony of consecrating; the state of being consecrated; dedication. Until the days of your consecration be at an end. Lev. viii. 33. Consecration makes not a place sacred, but only sol em ny declares it so. South.
One who consecrates; one who performs the rites by which apers on or thing is devoted or dedicated to sacred purposes. [written also consecrater.]
Of or pertaining to the act of consecration; dedicatory. The consecratory prayer. Bp. Burnet.
Following as a matter of course. Blount.
Following by consequence; consequent; deducible. [R.]"Consectary impieties." Sir T. brow ne.
To follow closely; to endeavor to overtake; to pursue. [Obs.]Bp. Burnet.

Having similarity of sequence; -- said of certain parallel progressions of two parts in a piece of harmony; as, consecutive fifths, or consecutive octaves, which are forbidden. consecutive chords (Mus.), chords of the same kind su ce ed ing one another without interruption.
In a consecutive manner; by way of sequence; successively.
The state or quality of being consecutive.

Existing, or made, by the mutual consent of two or more parties.

Consequent points,Consequent poles (Magnetism), a number of poles distributed under certain conditions, along the axis of a magnetized steel bar, which regularly has but the two poles at the extremities.
The quality of being consequential.
By consequence; by natural or logical sequence or connection.

Conservation, as from injury, defilement, or irregular use.[An act was] passed in 1866, for vesting in the Conservators of the river Thames the conservancy of the Thames and Isis. Mozley & W.
Having the power or quality of conservation.

The act of preserving, guarding, or protecting; the keeping (ofa thing) in a safe or entire state; preservation. A step necessary for the conservation of Protestantism. hall am. A state without the means of some change is without the means of its conservation. Burke. Conservation of areas (Astron.), the principle that the radius vector drawn from a planet to the sun sweeps over equal areas in equal times.-- Conservation of energy, or Conservation of force (Mech.), the principle that the total energy of any material system is a quantity which can neither be increased nor diminished by any action between the parts of the system, though it may be transformed into any of the forms of which energy is susceptible. Clerk Maxwell.
Tending to conserve; preservative.
The disposition and tendency to preserve what is established;opposition to change; the habit of mind; or conduct, of a conservative.
A member of the Conservative party.
The quality of being conservative.
A public place of instruction in any special branch, esp. music and the arts. [See Conservatory, 3].
Having the quality of preserving from loss, decay, or injury.
A woman who preserves from loss, injury, etc.
A medicinal confection made of freshly gathered vegetable substances mixed with finely powdered refined sugar. See Confection.
One who conserves.
Worthiness of consideration; dignity; value; size; amount.
In a manner or to a degree not trifling or unimportant;greatly; much. The breeds . . . differ considerably from each other. Darwin.

The cause which moves a contracting party to enter into an agreement; the material cause of a contract; the price of as trip ula ti on; compensation; equivalent. Bouvier.
Considerate; careful; thoughtful. [Archaic]I love to be considerative. B. jon son.

One who considers; a man of reflection; a thinker. Milton.

Having joint or equal signification; synonymous. [R.] Spelman.

In a consistent manner.

Pertaining to a Presbyterian consistory; -- a contemptuous term of 17th century controversy. You fall next on the consistorian schismatics; for so you call presbyterians. Milton.
The spiritual court of a diocesan bishop held before his chancellor or commissioner in his cathedral church or elsewhere. Hook.

A collection of maritime laws of disputed origin, supposed to have been first published at Barcelona early in the 14th century. it has formed the basis of most of the subsequent collections of maritime laws. Kent. Bouvier.
One who consoles or comforts. Johnson.
Of a consoling or comforting nature. The punishment of tyrants is a noble and awful act of justice; and it has with truth been said to be consolatory to the human mind. Burke.

To cheer in distress or depression; to alleviate the grief and raise the spirits of; to relieve; to comfort; to soothe. And empty heads console with empty sound. Pope. I am much consoled by the reflection that the religion of Christ has been attacked in vain by all the wits and philosophers, and its triumph has been complete. P. Henry.
One who gives consolation.
Serving to unite or consolidate; having the quality of consolidating or making firm.
Formed into a solid mass; made firm; consolidated. [R.]A gentleman [should learn to ride] while he is tender and the brawns and sinews of his thighs not fully consolidate. el yot.

Having a small surface in proportion to bulk, as in the cactus. Consolidated plants are evidently adapted and designed for very dry regions; in such only they are found. Gray. The Consolidated Fund, a British fund formed by consolidating (in1787) three public funds (the Aggregate Fund, the General Fund, and the South Sea Fund). In 1816, the larger part of the revenues of great br it ian and Ireland was assigned to what has been known as the consolidated Fund of the United Kingdom, out of which are paid the interest of the national debt, the salaries of the civil list, etc.
To organic cohesion of different circled in a flower; adnation.
Tending or having power to consolidate; healing.
Adapted to console or comfort; cheering; as, this is consoling news.
The leading British funded government security.
A clear soup or bouilli on boiled down so as to be very rich.
harmonizing together; accordant; as, consonant tones, consonant chords.
To change into, or use as, a consonant. "The vowel is consonantized, that is, made closer in position." pe ile.

Engaging in a plot to commit a crime; conspiring. [Obs.] sh ak.

Agreement or concurrence for some end or purpose; conspiracy.[R.]As soon as it was day, certain Jews made a conspiration. ud all. In our natural body every part has a na ca ss ary sympathy with every other, and all together form, by their harmonious on spiration, a healthy whole. Sir W. Hamilton.
One who engages in a conspiracy; a plotter. 2 Sam. xv. 31.
To plot; to plan; to combine for. Angry clouds conspire your overthrow. Bp. Hall.
One who conspires; a conspirator.
In the manner of a conspirator; by conspiracy. Milton.
A making thick or viscous; thickness; inspissation. [R.] Dr. H. More.
To pollute; to defile. [Obs.] cocker am.
This act of defiling; defilement; pollution. Bp. Hall.
An officer of the peace having power as a conservator of the public peace, and bound to ex eu te the warrants of judicial off ie rs. Bouvier.

The wife of a constable. [Obs.]
The district to which a constable's power is limited. [Obs.]Sir M. Hale.

With constancy; steadily; continually; perseveringly; without cessation; uniformly. But she constantly affirmed that it was even so. Acts. xii. 15.

To join luster; to shine with united radiance, or one general light. [R.]The several things which engage our affections . . . shine forth and constellate in God. Boule.

Amazement or horror that confounds the faculties, and incapacitates for ref let ion; terror, combined with am axe me nt; dismay. The chiefs around, In silence wrapped, in on st er nation downed. attend the stern reply. Pope.

A body of constituents, as the body of citizens or voters in are presentative district.
A person who appoints another to act for him as attorney in fact. burr ill.
An established law. [Obs.] T. pre st on.
One who constitutes or appoints.
A walk or other exercise taken for one's health or constitution. [Colloq.] thacker ay. The men trudged diurnal constitutionals along the different roads. com pt on re ade.
The theory, principles, or authority of constitutional government; attachment or ad here ne to a constitution or constitutional government. carl yle.
One who advocates a constitutional form of government; a constitutionalist.
One who adheres to the constitution of the country. bol ing broke.
In a constitutive manner.
Capable of being constrained; liable to constraint, or to restraint. Hooker.
Marked by constraint; not free; not voluntary; embarrassed; as,a constrained manner; a constrained tone.

One who constrains.

The act of constraining, or the state of being constrained;that which compels to, or restrains from, action; compulsion;restraint; necessity. Long imprisonment and hard constraint. sp en ser. Not by constraint, but bDryden.
Constraining; compulsory. [R.] "Any constraintive vow." R. car ew.

To draw together; to render narrower or smaller; to bind; to cramp; to contract or a use to shrink. Such things as constrict the fibers. ar bu th not. Membranous organs inclosing a cavity which their contraction constrict. Todd & Bowman.

In a constructive manner; by construction or inference. A neutral must have notice of a blockade, either actually by a formal information, or constructively by notice to his government. Kent.
The faculty which enables one to construct, as in mechanical,artistic, or literary matters.
A constructer.

Capable of being consumed; that may be destroyed, dissipated,wasted, or spent. "Consumable commodities." Locke.

In a consummate manner; completely. T. war ton.

The act of consummating, or the state of being consummated;completed; completion; perfection; termination; end (as of the world or of life)."Tis a consummation Devoutly to be wished. sh ak. Consumption of the bowels (Med.),inflammation and ulceration of the intestines from tubercular disease.

A state of being consumptive, or a tendency to a consumption.
Wasting away gradually. Darwin. - Con*ta*bes"cence, n.

The transmission of a disease from one person to another, by direct or indirect contact.
Affected by contagion.

Communicable by contact, by a virus, or by a bodily exhalation;catching; as, a contagious disease.

Most such diseases have already been proved to be germ diseases, and their communicability depends on the transmission of the living germs. Many germ diseases are not contagious, some special method of transmission or inoculation of the germs being required.
In a contagious manner.
Quality of being contagious.
Contagion; contagious matter. "Contagium of measles." tynd all.
To restrain desire; to live in continence or chastity. But if they can not contain, let them marry. 1 Cor. vii. 9.
